name: Scholarly Growth Reputation Institutional Memory Recordkeeping Crowding Out Qualification 4B71E2D0Aa
text: Santos, Cerqueira, and Carvalho Júnior provide an independent qualification of Kaal’s principle that reputation is institutional memory rather than merely a score. Their repeated trust-game study treats recordkeeping as externalized memory of past interactions, yet reports that introducing records in a direct-dyad setting reduced trust formation and reciprocity through a crowding-out mechanism. The result makes the memory layer analytically distinct from its behavioral output: preserving history does not itself guarantee cooperative effects. The study does not compare records with numerical scores and does not test Kaal’s agentic substrate.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: Basu et al. (2009) argue that this result occurs because recordkeeping, by complementing the resources of the brain, improves the memory of past interactions, meaning that the decisions regarding future interactions are conditioned by the partners’ history of cooperation.

The main result documented presents evidence that recordkeeping reduces the propensity to form trust and, as a result, negatively affects the direct reciprocity when only that type of mechanism for promoting cooperation is possible.

The results are robust for a variety of statistical tests, but they differ from the one originally presented by Basu et al. (2009), since, while the latter identified that recordkeeping increased reciprocity, by promoting reputation building, this study recorded a reduction in the level of direct reciprocity.

As Basu and Waymire (2006) clarify, accounting records institutionalize the memory of past transactions and, combined with norms of honesty incorporated into laws and other institutions, they serve to sustain the trust that enables reputation building and, consequently, cooperation between economic agents.
